# Managing billing for ChatGPT and the API platform

Find billing settings and support for your ChatGPT account, workspace, or API organization.

Updated: 9 days ago

# Overview

ChatGPT and the API platform have separate billing systems. Manage each product’s charges and billing history in its own settings.
API credits, including promotional API credits, are associated with an API organization. They are separate from your ChatGPT subscription and the credit balances used within ChatGPT.

# Manage billing for ChatGPT on the web

For Free, Go, Plus, or Pro accounts, open ChatGPT billing settings, or:

  1. Sign in to ChatGPT on the web.

  2. Open Settings.

  3. Select Billing.

If you subscribed on the web, use the options in Billing to manage your subscription, payment methods, and available billing history.

If billing or payment controls are missing, sign in to the same ChatGPT account in a different browser, then try opening your billing settings again.

# Manage ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, or Edu billing

For ChatGPT Business, workspace owners and admins can open Workspace settings > Billing. Only workspace owners can update billing information and payment methods or view invoices.

For eligible ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu workspaces, authorized workspace owners and admins can select their workspace in the Global Admin Console, then open Billing. Available controls depend on your plan and permissions. For eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces, owners can view issued invoices in Billing > Invoices. Other roles can view invoices if your workspace is configured to allow it.

# Manage API billing

API organization owners can view billing details in the API billing overview.
Eligible subscriptions may offer promotional credits for a linked API organization; ChatGPT and API billing remain separate. See API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions.

## Set up API billing separately from ChatGPT

To start paid API usage, add a payment method in your API account billing settings. API usage is billed separately from your ChatGPT subscription.

API charges depend on the models and features you use, including token usage and any applicable tool or storage charges. Check the API pricing page for current rates.

For prepaid credit purchases and automatic recharges, see: Setting up prepaid billing.

# Check subscriptions on more than one platform

ChatGPT subscriptions can be billed through the web, Apple App Store, or Google Play Store. Subscriptions on more than one platform may result in separate charges.

To identify which platform manages your subscription and avoid duplicate charges, see: Managing your ChatGPT subscription across devices.

# Get help with a billing issue

Browse the billing help collection for guidance on your issue.

If you can’t identify or resolve the problem, contact OpenAI Support using the chat widget in the Help Center.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Invoice dates for ChatGPT and API billing

Learn how billing and invoicing work for ChatGPT subscriptions and API usage.

Updated: 8 days ago

## Overview

OpenAI does not support changes to invoice dates. Billing cycles and invoice schedules depend on your subscription type and billing arrangement.

## ChatGPT subscriptions

For a self-serve ChatGPT subscription billed monthly:

  * Billing recurs on the date you subscribed.

  * For example, if you subscribed on the 12th, you are billed again on the 12th of each following month.

  * Invoice dates follow that recurring schedule and cannot be modified.

On a self-service ChatGPT Business plan, assigning an unused, already-paid Standard or Premium seat adds no charge. Adding paid seats can create a prorated charge between renewals. See how Business seat charges work.

## ChatGPT Enterprise billing

For ChatGPT Enterprise, your agreement sets the billing period and invoice schedule. The billing period may differ from a calendar month or the date you signed up. Check the period shown on your invoice before comparing it with usage reports.

For Enterprise agreements with token-based billing in USD, usage is billed monthly after the billing period ends. Monthly invoicing does not change your contract term. ChatGPT workspace billing and API Platform billing remain separate.

For an overview of the billing model, see: Token-based billing for ChatGPT Enterprise. For help with your invoice schedule or first invoice, contact your OpenAI account team.

## API billing

API billing is not always postpaid. Accounts can use prepaid credits or automatic card payments, while Enterprise API customers receive invoices.

### Enterprise API invoices

For Enterprise API customers, invoices cover calendar-month usage unless a different custom billing arrangement is agreed in writing. For example, an invoice covering March usage is issued after March ends.

Invoices are typically issued within 2 weeks after the billing cycle ends. Your Enterprise contract determines your payment terms.

You can download invoices from the Billing section of the API Platform.

To compare an Enterprise API invoice with usage, select the API organization and service dates shown on the invoice and export Cost data. If the invoice covers multiple organizations, include each one.

### Other API customers

If you use the API as an individual or team customer:

  * Payment is handled through prepaid credits or automatic credit-card charges.

  * You can view your payment history and available invoices or receipts in Billing history.

For automatic credit-card billing, payments are collected at usage thresholds or monthly, depending on your payment method and country.

For prepaid credit purchases and automatic recharges, see: Setting up and managing prepaid API billing.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Introducing Grok Build

Now in early beta for all SuperGrok and X Premium Plus subscribers — Grok Build is a new coding agent that runs right from your terminal.

Today we're launching an early beta of Grok Build, a powerful new coding agent for professional software engineering and complex coding work.

Available now to all SuperGrok and X Premium Plus subscribers. Install Grok Build with a single command and sign in with your account:

### Install Grok Build

`$ curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh | bash`

## Plan, review, approve

For complex tasks, start Grok Build in plan mode. You can approve the plan, comment on individual steps, or rewrite it entirely before execution begins. Once a plan is approved, every change shows up as a clean diff.

## Works with what you already use

Your AGENTS.md, plugins, hooks, skills, and MCP servers all work out of the box. Start Grok Build in your repo and it picks up your conventions instantly.

## Subagents that work in parallel

For larger tasks, Grok Build delegates work to specialized subagents that run in parallel. Grok Build also supports deep worktree integrations, and you can launch subagents in their own worktrees.

## Built to fit your workflow

Headless mode (`-p`) allows easily running agents inside scripts and automations. Grok Build also provides full ACP support to build your own  bots and agent orchestration apps.

## Try it today

This is an early beta, and your feedback is the fastest way to make it better. Type `/feedback` in Grok Build to send bugs, requests, and reactions straight to the team.

SuperGrok and X Premium Plus subscribers can install Grok Build with the command above and start building. If you don't have SuperGrok yet, upgrade here — we're excited to see what you create.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Overview

OpenAI does not support changes to invoice dates. Billing cycles and invoice schedules depend on your subscription type and billing arrangement.

# ChatGPT subscriptions

For a self-serve ChatGPT subscription billed monthly:

  * Billing recurs on the date you subscribed.

  * For example, if you subscribed on the 12th, you are billed again on the 12th of each following month.

  * Invoice dates follow that recurring schedule and cannot be modified.

# ChatGPT Enterprise billing

For ChatGPT Enterprise, your agreement sets the billing period and invoice schedule. The billing period may differ from a calendar month or the date you signed up. Check the period shown on your invoice before comparing it with usage reports.
For Enterprise agreements with token-based billing in USD, usage is billed monthly after the billing period ends. Monthly invoicing does not change your contract term. ChatGPT workspace billing and API Platform billing remain separate.
For an overview of the billing model, see: Token-based billing for ChatGPT Enterprise. For help with your invoice schedule or first invoice, contact your OpenAI account team.

# API billing

API billing is not always postpaid. Accounts can use prepaid credits or automatic card payments, while Enterprise API customers receive invoices.

For Enterprise API customers, invoices cover calendar-month usage unless a different custom billing arrangement is agreed in writing. For example, an invoice covering March usage is issued after March ends.

For invoice availability, timing, and receipts, see: API billing and invoice timing.

# Monthly API credits for Max, Ultra, and Team plans

Max, Ultra, and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.

Available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.

## Monthly credits by plan

Plan  | Monthly credit
Max  | $100
Ultra  | $200
Team (Standard seats)  | $20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)  | $100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)  | $20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*

*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.

## Eligibility

  * Active plan. 
  * Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web

  * Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork

  * Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry


## How the credits work

  * Refreshes each billing cycle. New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.

  * Doesn't roll over. Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.

  * Used first. Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.

  * Shared across the organization. Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.

  * Separate from your plan limits. The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.

  * Visible in the Console. All credits appear on the Billing page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.

## What happens when your credits run out

  * If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload, usage continues and draws from those.

# Use Grok in OpenClaw

Use your SuperGrok or X Premium subscription inside OpenClaw, an open-source, local-first agent and personal assistant.

Starting today, log in and use your SuperGrok or X Premium subscription inside OpenClaw.

OpenClaw is an open-source, local-first agent and personal assistant. It runs on any hardware — a Mac Mini, laptop, server, VPS, or even a Raspberry Pi — and keeps persistent memory across sessions.

OpenClaw connects to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, and many other messaging platforms, so you can interact with your agent wherever you already chat.

If you already have a Grok or X Premium subscription, you can now use Grok models inside OpenClaw. Connecting Grok to your OpenClaw agent is available on every tier.

## Setup

Install OpenClaw:

[Button: macOS / Linux][Button: Windows]

Copy
    
    `curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash
    `

Run the guided onboarding:

Copy
    
    `openclaw onboard --install-daemon
    `

bash

On a VPS or over SSH, use device-code. OpenClaw prints a short code and URL you can open in any browser to finish sign-in:

Copy
    
    `openclaw onboard --auth-choice xai-device-code
    `

bash

Or connect a messaging app — Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, and more — and talk to your agent there.

For more, see OpenClaw getting started and the xAI provider docs.

L53: ## Who can link an app
L54: 
L55: Your organization must be billed directly by Anthropic, and only a user with the Admin or Billing role in your organization can approve a connection. If you don't have one of these roles, pass the request to someone who does. Learn more about 【19†Claude Console roles and permissions】.
L56: 
L57: The following can't be linked:
L58: 
L59:   * Organizations that get Claude through a cloud provider, such as Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Foundry, can't link
L60:   * Claude subscription plans (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise) can't be linked
L61: 
L62:   * Claude Console organizations that pay through the AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure marketplace can’t use linked billing
L63: 
L64: If you don't have a Claude account or Claude Console organization yet, you can create them for free while you link. Add credits before the app makes requests.
L65: One approval covers your whole organization. The link belongs to the organization, so it stays active if the approver leaves. Your organization can have one link per app.
L66: ## Link an app
L67: 
L68: To link an app:
L69: 
L70:   1. In the app, click the button to link your Claude organization.
L71: 
L72:   2. Sign in to Claude. If you have more than one organization, pick the one to link.
L73: 
L74:   3. Read how billing works, then set a monthly spend limit or select "Continue without a limit." If the app is still in testing, you must set a limit of $50 or less.
L75:   4. Review the approval screen. It shows the app's name and asks for permission to bill your organization for the Claude requests the app makes for you. It also says usage is billed under your organization's existing billing terms.
L76: 
L77:   5. Select "Link and authorize." You return to the app.
L78: 
L79: Your organization's Admin and Billing members usually get an email that confirms the link.
L80: ## Set a spend limit
L81: 
L82: Set a monthly limit (Console calls this a spend cap) for each app on the 【20†Linked platforms†platform.claude.com】 page in the Claude Console. You can also set a default limit that applies to each app separately. It isn’t a shared cap across apps.
L83: 
L84: To set a limit for one app, open its page under Linked platforms. A limit set there replaces your default limit. Your organization's own monthly limit is under Spend limits.
L85: Limits are optional and in US dollars. The exception is an app in testing, which needs a limit of $50 or less. Set a whole-dollar amount from $1, or $0 to refuse every request from the app. Your organization's own monthly limit still applies, and requests are refused when you reach either one.
L86: 
L87: When you reach the limit, requests from that app are refused until you raise it or the month resets on the 1st (UTC).
L88: The limit isn't exact. The request that crosses the limit is still served, and calls already running also finish, so your total can end up a little above the limit.
L89: 
L90: Your organization's admins get an email when usage in an app reaches 80% of the limit, and another at 100%. A $0 limit sends no email. Some organizations don't get these emails.
L91: 
L92: Usage is counted at list price. It includes tokens and web searches. The amount counted can differ from the amount on your invoice.
L93: ## Unlink an app
L94: 
L95: A user with the Admin or Billing role can unlink an app on the 【20†Linked platforms†platform.claude.com】 page. An app may also let you unlink from inside it. The app's team can unlink it from their side. However the link ends, the app then shows as Unlinked on that page.
L96: 
L97: If you unlink the app, your organization's Admin and Billing members usually get an email. If the app's team unlinks it, they may not get one.
L98: New calls usually stop within about 10 seconds. Calls already running finish and are billed to your organization. Past usage stays in Usage and Billing. To link the app again, approve the connection.
L99: ## How linked usage is billed
L100: 
L101: Anthropic bills linked usage, not the app. Any subscription the app charges is billed separately by the app. Learn more about 【21†how to pay for your Claude API usage】.
L102: 
L103: Linked usage is billed to your organization's prepaid balance or invoice. Some promotional credits can't be used.
L104: 
L105: ### What can pay
L106: 
L107:   * Credit you've purchased (your prepaid balance)
L108: 
L109:   * Your invoice, if you're billed monthly
L110: 
L111:   * Billing corrections from Anthropic
L112: 
L113:   * Credits written into your agreement
L114: ### What can't pay
L115: 
L116:   * 【22†Monthly API credits that come with Max, Ultra, and Team plans】
L117: 
L118:   * Sign-up credits limited to specific products
L119: 
L120:   * Credits from Anthropic's partner, venture capital, and startup programs (we're still rolling this out)
L121: ### What to expect
L122: 
L123:   * If nothing on your account can pay, the app's requests may be refused. After you add funds, the purchase can take some time to apply.
L124: 
L125:   * Your purchased balance may go down while a promotional balance stays the same.
L126: 
L127:   * We may update this list as our credit programs change.
L128: 
L129: ## View linked usage
L130: 
L131: The Linked platforms page in the Console lists each linked app, and you can set limits and unlink there. The page also shows what each app has cost you this month.
L132: ## Frequently asked questions
L133: 
L134: ### Can my organization link if it has HIPAA, FERPA, or CMEK requirements?
L135: 
L136: Not during the beta. Linked requests run in the app's organization, so your organization's business associate agreement (BAA), encryption keys, and retention settings, including zero data retention, don't apply.

L253: Claude Code securely manages your authentication credentials:

L255:     * On macOS, credentials are stored in the encrypted macOS Keychain. A Console login that creates an API key fails until the Keychain is writable. To move your login back into the Keychain, follow 【68†the recovery steps】.
L256:     * On Linux, credentials are stored in `~/.claude/.credentials.json` with file mode `0600`.
L257:     * On Windows, credentials are stored in `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\.credentials.json` and inherit the access controls of your user profile directory, which restricts the file to your user account by default.

L4: # Authentication with OAuth quickstart
L5: 
L6: The easiest way to authenticate to the Gemini API is to configure an API
L7: key, as described in the [Gemini API get started
L8: guide](/docs/get-started). If you need stricter access controls,
L9: you can use OAuth instead. This guide will help
L10: you set up authentication with OAuth.
L11: This guide uses a simplified authentication approach that is appropriate
L12: for a testing environment. For a production environment, learn
L13: about
L14: [authentication and authorization](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/auth-overview)
L15: before
L16: [choosing the access credentials](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/create-credentials#choose_the_access_credential_that_is_right_for_you)
L17: that are appropriate for your app.
L18: ## Objectives  {% id="objectives" %}
L19: 
L20: * Set up your cloud project for OAuth
L21: * Set up application-default-credentials
L22: * Manage credentials in your program instead of using `gcloud auth`
L23: 
L24: ## Prerequisites  {% id="prerequisites" %}
L25: 
L26: To run this quickstart, you need:
L27: 
L28: * [A Google Cloud project](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/create-project)
L29: * [A local installation of the gcloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install)
L30: ## Set up your cloud project  {% id="set-cloud" %}
L31: 
L32: To complete this quickstart, you first need to setup your Cloud project.
L33: 
L34: ### 1. Enable the API  {% id="enable-api" %}
L35: 
L36: Before using Google APIs, you need to turn them on in a Google Cloud project.
L37: 
L38: * In the Google Cloud console, enable the Google Generative Language API.
L39: 
L40:   {% button href="https://console.cloud.google.com/flows/enableapi?apiid=generativelanguage.googleapis.com" variant="primary" %}Enable the API{% /button %}
L41: ### 2. Configure the OAuth consent screen  {% id="configure-oauth" %}
L42: 
L43: Next configure the project's OAuth consent screen and add yourself as a test
L44: user. If you've already completed this step for your Cloud project, skip to the
L45: next section.
L46: 
L47: 1. In the Google Cloud console, go to **Menu** >
L48:    **Google Auth platform** > **Overview**.
L49: 
L50: {% button href="https://console.developers.google.com/auth/overview" variant="primary" %}Go to the Google Auth platform{% /button %}
L51: 1. Complete the project configuration form and set the user type to **External**
L52:    in the **Audience** section.
L53: 
L54: 2. Complete the rest of the form, accept the User Data Policy terms, and then
L55:    click **Create**.
L56: 
L57: 3. For now, you can skip adding scopes and click **Save and Continue**. In the
L58:    future, when you create an app for use outside of your Google Workspace
L59:    organization, you must add and verify the authorization scopes that your
L60:    app requires.
L61: 
L62: 4. Add test users:
L63:    1.  Navigate to the
L64:        [Audience page](https://console.developers.google.com/auth/audience) of the
L65:        Google Auth platform.
L66: 
L67:    2.  Under **Test users**, click **Add users**.
L68: 
L69:    3.  Enter your email address and any other authorized test users, then
L70:        click **Save**.
L71: ### 3. Authorize credentials for a desktop application  {% id="authorize-credentials" %}
L72: 
L73: To authenticate as an end user and access user data in your app, you need to
L74: create one or more OAuth 2.0 Client IDs. A client ID is used to identify a
L75: single app to Google's OAuth servers. If your app runs on multiple platforms,
L76: you must create a separate client ID for each platform.
L77: 
L78: 1. In the Google Cloud console, go to **Menu** > **Google Auth platform** >
L79:    **Clients**.
L80: {% button href="https://console.developers.google.com/auth/clients" variant="primary" %}Go to Credentials{% /button %}
L81: 
L82: 1. Click **Create Client**.
L83: 
L84: 2. Click **Application type** > **Desktop app**.
L85: 
L86: 3. In the **Name** field, type a name for the credential. This name is only
L87:    shown in the Google Cloud console.
L88: 
L89: 4. Click **Create**. The OAuth client created screen appears, showing your new
L90:    Client ID and Client secret.
L91: 5. Click **OK**. The newly created credential appears under **OAuth 2.0 Client
L92:    IDs.**
L93: 
L94: 6. Click the download button to save the JSON file. It will be saved as
L95:    `client_secret_<identifier>.json`, and rename it to `client_secret.json`
L96:    and move it to your working directory.
L97: ## Set up Application Default Credentials  {% id="set-application-default" %}
L98: 
L99: To convert the `client_secret.json` file into usable credentials, pass its
L100: location the `gcloud auth application-default login` command's
L101: `--client-id-file` argument.
L102: 
L103: ```posix-terminal
L104: gcloud auth application-default login \
L105:     --client-id-file=client_secret.json \
L106:     --scopes='https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/generative-language.retriever'
L107: ```
L108: The simplified project setup in this tutorial triggers a **"Google hasn't
L109: verified this app."** dialog. This is normal, choose **"continue"**.
L110: 
L111: This places the resulting token in a well known location so it can be accessed
L112: by `gcloud` or the client libraries.
L113: {% callout type="note" %}
L114:   Note: If running on Colab include `--no-browser` and carefully follow the
L115:   instructions it prints (don't just click the link). Also make sure your local
L116:   `gcloud --version` is the
L117:   [latest](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/release-notes) to match Colab.
L118: 
L119: {% /callout %}
L120: ```bash
L121: gcloud auth application-default login \
L122:     --no-browser \
L123:     --client-id-file=client_secret.json \
L124:     --scopes='https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/generative-language.retriever'
L125: ```
L126: 
L127: Once you have the Application Default Credentials (ADC) set, the client
L128: libraries in most languages need minimal to no help to find them.
L129: ### Curl  {% id="curl" %}
L130: 
L131: The quickest way to test that this is working is to use it to access the REST
L132: API using curl:
L133: 
L134: ```posix-terminal
L135: access_token=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)
L136: project_id=<MY PROJECT ID>
L137: 
L138: curl -X GET https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1/models \
L139:     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
L140:     -H "Authorization: Bearer ${access_token}" \
L141:     -H "x-goog-user-project: ${project_id}" | grep '"name"'
L142: ```
L143: ### Python  {% id="python" %}
L144: 
L145: In python the client libraries should find them automatically:
L146: 
L147: ```bash
L148: pip install google-genai
L149: ```
L150: 
L151: A minimal script to test it might be:
L152: 
L153: ```python
L154: from google import genai
L155: 
L156: client = genai.Client()
L157: print('Available base models:', [m.name for m in client.models.list()])
L158: ```
L159: ## Manage credentials yourself [Python]  {% id="manage-credentials" %}
L160: In many cases you won't have the `gcloud` command available to create the access
L161: token from the Client ID (`client_secret.json`). Google provides libraries in
L162: many languages to let you manage that process within your app. This section
L163: demonstrates the process, in python. There are equivalent examples of this sort
L164: of procedure, for other languages, available in the
L165: [Drive API documentation](https://developers.google.com/drive/api/quickstart/python)
L166: ### 1. Install the necessary libraries  {% id="install-libs" %}
L167: 
L168: Install the Google client library for Python, and the Gemini client library.
L169: 
L170: ```posix-terminal
L171: pip install --upgrade -q google-api-python-client google-auth-httplib2 google-auth-oauthlib
L172: 
L173: pip install google-genai
L174: ```
L175: ### 2. Write the credential manager  {% id="write-credentials" %}
L176: 
L177: To minimize the number of times you have to click through the authorization
L178: screens, create a file called `load_creds.py` in your working directory to
L179: caches a `token.json` file that it can reuse later, or refresh if it expires.
L180: 
L181: Start with the
L182: following code to convert the `client_secret.json` file to a token usable with
L183: `genai.configure`:
L184: 
L185: ```python
L186: import os.path
L187: from google.auth.transport.requests import Request
L188: from google.oauth2.credentials import Credentials
L189: from google_auth_oauthlib.flow import InstalledAppFlow
L190: 
L191: SCOPES = ['https://www.googleapis.com/auth/generative-language.retriever']
L192: 
L193: def load_creds():
L194:     """Converts `client_secret.json` to a credential object.
L195:     This function caches the generated tokens to minimize the use of the
L196:     consent screen.
L197:     """
L198:     creds = None
L199:     # The file token.json stores the user's access and refresh tokens, and is
L200:     # created automatically when the authorization flow completes for the first
L201:     # time.
L202:     if os.path.exists('token.json'):
L203:         creds = Credentials.from_authorized_user_file('token.json', SCOPES)
L204:     # If there are no (valid) credentials available, let the user log in.
L205:     if not creds or not creds.valid:
L206:         if creds and creds.expired and creds.refresh_token:
L207:             creds.refresh(Request())
L208:         else:
L209:             flow = InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file(
L210:                 'client_secret.json', SCOPES)
L211:             creds = flow.run_local_server(port=0)
L212:         # Save the credentials for the next run
L213:         with open('token.json', 'w') as token:
L214:             token.write(creds.to_json())
L215:     return creds
L216: ```
L217: ### 3. Write your program  {% id="write-program" %}
L218: 
L219: Now create your `script.py`:
L220: 
L221: ```python
L222: import pprint
L223: from google import genai
L224: from load_creds import load_creds
L225: 
L226: creds = load_creds()
L227: 
L228: client = genai.Client(credentials=creds)
L229: 
L230: print()
L231: print('Available base models:', [m.name for m in client.models.list()])
L232: ```
L233: ### 4. Run your program  {% id="run-program" %}
L234: 
L235: In your working directory, run the sample:
L236: 
L237: ```posix-terminal
L238: python script.py
L239: ```
L240: 
L241: The first time you run the script, it opens a browser window and prompts you
L242: to authorize access.
L243: 
L244: 1. If you're not already signed in to your Google Account, you're prompted to
L245:    sign in. If you're signed in to multiple accounts, **be sure to select the
L246:    account you set as a "Test Account" when configuring your project.**
L247: {% callout type="note" %}
L248:   Note: The simplified project setup in this tutorial triggers a **"Google
L249:   hasn't verified this app."** dialog. This is normal, choose **"continue"**.
L250: 
L251: {% /callout %}
L252: 
L253: 1. Authorization information is stored in the file system, so the next time you
L254:    run the sample code, you aren't prompted for authorization.
L255: 
L256: You have successfully setup authentication.

L950: # Accounts and sessions
L951: 
L952: Copy Page
L953: 
L954: Manage ChatGPT accounts, renew access, sign out, and protect credentials.
L955: ## Managing ChatGPT accounts
L956: 
L957: Your app needs to manage multiple account registrations so users can choose an existing ChatGPT account or add another. Keep each registration’s basic account info, issued client ID, and credentials separate, even when two registrations have the same email address. Use distinct, stable labels and show the active ChatGPT account in the app’s account picker.
L958: When signing in again to the same account on the same host, reuse the registration’s issued `client_id` and stable `ext_agent_host_id`. Signing out or switching back to a saved ChatGPT account does not create a new client. See 【567†Store credentials in a local file】 for the credential record format and storage details.
L959: ## Switching ChatGPT accounts
L960: 
L961: Keep each registration’s issued client ID and credentials separate. Email helps users recognize an account but may be identical across account registrations. Use a distinct, stable label for each account registration, and keep its issued client ID associated with the validated ID-token identity.
L962: Reauthorization: Use the same authorize endpoint with the selected account’s issued `client_id` and fresh `state`, `nonce`, and PKCE values. Omit your app’s `agent_name_hint` from reauthorization requests. Include this host’s stable `ext_agent_host_id`. Send a retained `id_token` as `id_token_hint`; a saved email may also be sent as `login_hint`. Under the 【568†expected returning sign-in】, `id_token_hint` skips the unified session selector.
L963: It does not change the workspace bound to this client or replace validation of the newly issued ID token. Follow 【569†Validate the ID token and ChatGPT plan permission】 before replacing credentials.
L964: Within your OSS app, you may choose to offer an account picker that allows the user to:
L965:   * Continue with a saved ChatGPT account: Repeat OAuth with that account’s issued `client_id` and fresh state, nonce, and PKCE values. Keep the same host ID. Include retained login hints.
L966:   * Use a different ChatGPT account: Select its existing registration or register a new one with `client_id=dynamic_agent_client`. Switching accounts does not require signing out of every other saved account.
L967:   * Sign out: Stop requests. Attempt 【570†End the renewable session】 below before clearing the selected account’s access, refresh, and ID tokens. Retain its account/client mapping and this host’s ID for a later sign-in.
L968: Display the active ChatGPT account in settings or the account menu. Complete and validate the selected account’s OAuth flow before making it active. Never overwrite another account registration’s credentials or combine one registration’s client ID with another registration’s tokens.
L969: ### End the renewable session
L970: 
L971: When signing out, revoke the renewable session using the `revocation_endpoint` from `https://auth.openai.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Send a form-encoded `POST` with `token=<REFRESH_TOKEN>`, `token_type_hint=refresh_token`, and the issued `client_id`. An empty HTTP `200` is the revocation success response, including for an already-invalid token. Stop using the tokens and clear them locally after revocation.
L972: For a network failure or `5xx`, retry with backoff while the refresh token is still available. If you finish signing out locally without confirming revocation, clear the local tokens and tell the user that remote revocation was not confirmed. The user can disconnect the app in ChatGPT Settings. Revoking this session does not delete the registered client.
L973: ## Refreshing tokens
L974: 
L975: Use standard OAuth refresh near access-token expiry. POST form-encoded `grant_type=refresh_token`, the issued `client_id` saved with this token set (not `dynamic_agent_client`), the saved `refresh_token`, and `resource=https://api.openai.com/v1` to `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token`; omit `scope` to retain the grant.
L976: 
L977: Store and use the latest replacement, and serialize refreshes for the same session so two processes do not race a rotating token.
L978: See 【571†Token lifetimes】 for expiry and renewal limits, and 【572†Refresh errors】 for recovery.
L979: ## Credential security
L980: 
L981: Keep access, refresh, and retained ID tokens in protected local or self-hosted runtime storage. Keep tokens out of browser storage, source control, logs, analytics, and support transcripts.
L982: 
L983: Never put access or refresh tokens in URLs. Send an ID token as `id_token_hint` only to the OpenAI authorization endpoint, and redact authorization URLs containing that hint from logs and diagnostics. A host ID is an opaque identifier, not a token or proof of identity.

## Understand scopes

With the appropriate identity scopes, your application can receive a stable account identifier and a person’s name, email address, and profile picture. Identity scopes don’t grant access to ChatGPT conversations or OpenAI API resources.

Using a ChatGPT plan requires separate Responses API scopes that the user must authorize. It doesn’t grant access to the user’s API key or conversations. Follow the open-source sign-in guide for its authorization and request contract.

## Follow the sign-in flow

Identity-only clients request `openid profile email` to receive an ID token for sign-in. Clients that use ChatGPT plans also request scopes for Responses API access. If the user grants those scopes, the token response includes an access token for eligible inference requests.

  1. Your application starts an OpenID Connect sign-in with PKCE.
  2. The person authenticates and consents with OpenAI.
  3. OpenAI returns an authorization code to your registered callback.
  4. Your backend exchanges the code and verifies the OpenAI ID token.
  5. Your application identifies or creates a local account and issues its own session.

For a plugin, your application also returns a connector authorization code to ChatGPT. The connector’s permissions and credentials remain separate from the OpenAI identity token.

Your application owns account creation, enterprise sign-in policy, sessions, authorization, and connector access. Sign in with ChatGPT supplies the verified OpenAI identity used by those application flows.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

+### Provider terms and credential lifecycles
+
+**OpenAI.** The Sign in with ChatGPT terms effective November 4 say “Do not impersonate OpenAI, another application or entity, or another open-source project.” The terms also require persistent token storage to be “local and under the user’s control”. For plan usage, requests must originate on the user's local runtime or a remote runtime the user alone controls. User authorization and app-specific use are required, and users must be able to use their plan in the app for free. A shared Betterlook backend with persistent token storage needs an approved design from OpenAI. The hosted identity-only flow uses authorization code with PKCE, state, nonce, and `openid profile email`. It returns an ID token for a Betterlook session and supplies no inference credential. Public website docs give no commercial plan-token lifecycle. [Sign in with ChatGPT terms §1 and §3.1](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), [website integration](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/website), [client request](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/request-client-id)
+
+The public OSS plan flow adds `offline_access resource.invoke chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`. Access tokens last one hour. Refresh tokens rotate with a fresh 30-day lifetime, and refreshes must be serialized per session. On sign-out revoke the refresh token at the discovery document's revocation endpoint and clear credentials. Users can disconnect in ChatGPT settings. The documented returning OSS flow uses an ID-token hint at the authorization endpoint, so confirm a supported returning flow that satisfies Betterlook's rule against any token in a URL. Inference uses eligible models on the public Responses API with `store: false` and `stream: true`. Check model availability and the request contract with AI-CORE if selected. +
+**Anthropic.** Claude Code's credential policy says “Anthropic does not permit third-party developers to offer Claude.ai login into their own applications”. It also forbids routing requests on behalf of users through consumer plan credentials and collecting or storing their Claude.ai session tokens. Claude Code's own sign-in and the compliant hosted-binary option leave the token with the official binary. Public docs describe its local credential storage and logout. Third-party consumer scopes, expiry, refresh, and revocation are therefore unavailable to Betterlook. [Authentication and credential use](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance#authentication-and-credential-use), [Claude Code credential management](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication#credential-management)
+
+For Claude Platform linked billing, request `billing:attribution` and add `offline_access` only for renewal. Connection tokens have `workspace:inference` and last at most one hour. The rotating refresh token has an absolute limit of one year, reported in `refresh_token_expires_in`. Serialize refreshes and follow Anthropic's retry rules. Revoke by connection ID through the OAuth revoke endpoint, or unlink in Claude Console. Both the access credential and the connection ID must be available during the connection lifecycle. A shared operator also needs explicit billing attribution on model requests. [OAuth reference](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/oauth-apps/oauth-reference), [linked billing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/oauth-apps/organization-billing-connections), [app review](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/oauth-apps/app-review)

+Desktop tools can invoke an official CLI on the user's machine and let it handle browser sign-in and credential storage. A hosted subprocess still needs explicit provider support and an approved way to isolate the user's execution and session. [Codex authentication](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth), [Codex app-server](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/codex-app-server), [Claude Code hosted terms](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance#can-customers-offer-claude-code-in-their-products), [Grok Build](https://docs.x.ai/build/overview), [Antigravity terms](https://www.antigravity.google/terms)

# AGENTS.md

Rules for every coding agent on Betterlook, Claude and Codex alike. Claude Code reads this through `CLAUDE.md`.

Read `PROBLEM.md` before any task. It decides scope, and where anything conflicts with it, it wins.

## What this is

Betterlook is a web visual editor. A designer describes a UI change in plain language, an agent edits the real code of their React app, and Betterlook checks the edit before the designer is told it worked. It is built from scratch: Onlook is the product we improve on, not a codebase we use. No Onlook code, dependencies or docs are copied in.

## Product rules

- **An MVP.** Build what `PROBLEM.md` needs and nothing else. Deletion over addition.
- **No failure, no work.** A new check, metric, judge, fixture or feature names the observed failure that drove it: a trace, or a row in `PROBLEM.md`'s failure table. Without one, it isn't built.
- **Eval order.** Read traces, then name the failure, then a deterministic check (build, diff scope, rendered UI). A judge comes only where code can't decide, and only after it agrees with human labels.
- **Humans write the eval content.** Rubrics, judge prompts, golden labels and safety fixtures are written by the team. A coding agent builds the harness that runs them, and never writes or edits their content. Where a task needs one, leave a clearly empty slot and say so in the handoff.
- **Reliability is `pass^k`.** One passing run proves nothing. Report pass^k over a frozen suite, per model.
- **Hidden machinery.** The designer sees the edit and its outcome. Evals, traces and judges add no screen, control or setting to the designer's UI.
- **Keys stay the user's.** Users bring their own model keys. Keys are never logged, traced, committed or sent anywhere but their provider. Traces redact secrets before they are written to disk.
- **No training.** Nothing fine-tunes, distils or trains on user data.
- **English only.** No translations, no changesets.

## Code rules

- **Understand, then reuse.** Trace the behaviour end to end and fix the root cause. Before writing anything, reuse what the repo already has, then the standard library, then the platform, then an installed dependency. Add a dependency only when none of those can do it, and say why in the handoff.
- **Task-only diff.** Change only what the task needs: no renames, reformatting or cleanup of nearby code.
- **Tests.** A reproducible bug gets a failing test first, then the fix. Non-trivial logic leaves one small test behind. No new test framework.
- **Verify twice.** Run the checks in two separate clean runs before handing off. Both must pass.
- **No speculative code.** No abstraction with one user, no config for a value that never changes, no scaffolding for later.
- **Comments.** None by default. One short line only when it prevents a likely mistake a better name can't.
- **Docs** state present-tense rules, and change in the same commit as the code that makes them wrong.
- **Commits:** `type(scope): what changed`, present tense. Types `feat|fix|chore|docs|test|refactor|perf|build|ci`. No AI, model or tool attribution in commits, PRs, branch names or code.
- **Nothing private in the tree:** no keys, emails, personal names or internal links.

Claude sessions apply these through the `carmy` and `ponytail` skills and run `ponytail-review` on the diff before handoff. Codex sessions apply them through `carmy`. Any React change runs `npx react-doctor@latest` and fixes what it reports. Outside research uses `agent-reach`, and any claim that drives a decision cites its source.

## Working as one of several agents

Several agents work on Betterlook at once, each in its own workspace and branch, coordinated by an orchestrator.

- One task, one branch. Change only the files your task names. If you need to touch another file, stop and report it as blocked.
- Never merge, rebase onto, or push to the base branch. The orchestrator integrates.
- Commit on your branch only when your task says to.

SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE
task: <task-id>
summary: <one-line outcome>
files: <comma-separated paths or none>
checks: <commands and outcomes, both runs>
handoff: <next-step context or none>
```

```text

task: <task-id>
reason: <specific blocker>
needs: <decision, access, or dependency required>

# PROBLEM.md

The problem Betterlook solves. Every change in this repository serves it. When a doc, a habit or an Onlook feature conflicts with this file, this file wins.

## Statement

**Betterlook** is a visual editor where designers describe a UI change in plain language and an AI agent edits the real code of their React app. Onlook already makes the edit. It does not know whether the edit was good. Today an edit can break the build, touch code outside the request, regress the layout, behave differently on a second run, or follow an instruction hidden in a file or web page, and the designer is the one who finds out.

**We are handling evals.** The job is to make Betterlook's agent measurably controlled and confident, without the designer seeing any of the machinery:

- Learn how the agent actually fails by reading real traces, before choosing any metric.
- Check every edit against the real outcome (build, diff scope, rendered UI) with deterministic checks first, and narrow, human-calibrated judges only where code can't decide.
- Block regressions before merge, and measure reliability across repeated runs (`pass^k`), not one lucky run.
- Trace every session with secrets redacted, so real failures become new test cases.
- Prove that prompt and harness changes improve the agent on a frozen suite, across the models users choose.

## Constraints

- No model training of any kind.
- Users bring their own model keys.
- The team writes every rubric, judge, label and safety fixture by hand.
- The frontend is a new minimal Astryx shell.
- Cut anything not driven by an observed failure.

## The failures we know of

These are the failures the statement names. A new one joins this list only from a real trace.

| Failure | What the designer sees today |
|---|---|
| Build breaks | The app stops rendering after the edit. |
| Out-of-scope diff | Files or code the request never mentioned changed. |
| Layout regression | Something other than the requested element moved or broke. |
| Nondeterminism | The same request gives a different result on a second run. |
| Prompt injection | The agent followed an instruction found in a file or web page, not the designer's. |

## Done means

- A designer's edit is checked against the build, the diff and the rendered UI before they are told it worked.
- A prompt or harness change merges only if it does no worse on the frozen suite, measured as `pass^k`, on every model users can pick.
- Every session leaves a redacted trace, and a failure found in one can become a test case.
- None of this adds a screen, a control or a wait the designer has to manage.

## Decisions

- Betterlook is a web app, built from scratch, frontend and agent backend alike. No Onlook code is reused; Onlook is only the product we measure against.
- English only. No translations, no changesets.

# AGENTS.md

Rules for every coding agent on Betterlook, Claude and Codex alike. Claude Code reads this through `CLAUDE.md`.

Read `PROBLEM.md` before any task. It decides scope, and where anything conflicts with it, it wins.

## What this is

Betterlook is a web visual editor. A designer describes a UI change in plain language, an agent edits the real code of their React app, and Betterlook checks the edit before the designer is told it worked. It is built from scratch: Onlook is the product we improve on, not a codebase we use. No Onlook code, dependencies or docs are copied in.

## Product rules

- **An MVP.** Build what `PROBLEM.md` needs and nothing else. Deletion over addition.
- **No failure, no work.** A new check, metric, judge, fixture or feature names the observed failure that drove it: a trace, or a row in `PROBLEM.md`'s failure table. Without one, it isn't built.
- **Eval order.** Read traces, then name the failure, then a deterministic check (build, diff scope, rendered UI). A judge comes only where code can't decide, and only after it agrees with human labels.
- **Humans write the eval content.** Rubrics, judge prompts, golden labels and safety fixtures are written by the team. A coding agent builds the harness that runs them, and never writes or edits their content. Where a task needs one, leave a clearly empty slot and say so in the handoff.
- **Reliability is `pass^k`.** One passing run proves nothing. Report pass^k over a frozen suite, per model.
- **Hidden machinery.** The designer sees the edit and its outcome. Evals, traces and judges add no screen, control or setting to the designer's UI.
- **Keys stay the user's.** Users bring their own model keys. Keys are never logged, traced, committed or sent anywhere but their provider. Traces redact secrets before they are written to disk.
- **No training.** Nothing fine-tunes, distils or trains on user data.
- **English only.** No translations, no changesets.

## Code rules

- **Understand, then reuse.** Trace the behaviour end to end and fix the root cause. Before writing anything, reuse what the repo already has, then the standard library, then the platform, then an installed dependency. Add a dependency only when none of those can do it, and say why in the handoff.
- **Task-only diff.** Change only what the task needs: no renames, reformatting or cleanup of nearby code.
- **Tests.** A reproducible bug gets a failing test first, then the fix. Non-trivial logic leaves one small test behind. No new test framework.
- **Verify twice.** Run the checks in two separate clean runs before handing off. Both must pass.
- **No speculative code.** No abstraction with one user, no config for a value that never changes, no scaffolding for later.
- **Comments.** None by default. One short line only when it prevents a likely mistake a better name can't.
- **Docs** state present-tense rules, and change in the same commit as the code that makes them wrong.
- **Commits:** `type(scope): what changed`, present tense. Types `feat|fix|chore|docs|test|refactor|perf|build|ci`. No AI, model or tool attribution in commits, PRs, branch names or code.
- **Nothing private in the tree:** no keys, emails, personal names or internal links.

Claude sessions apply these through the `carmy` and `ponytail` skills and run `ponytail-review` on the diff before handoff. Codex sessions apply them through `carmy`. Any React change runs `npx react-doctor@latest` and fixes what it reports. Outside research uses `agent-reach`, and any claim that drives a decision cites its source.

## Working as one of several agents

Several agents work on Betterlook at once, each in its own workspace and branch, coordinated by an orchestrator.

- One task, one branch. Change only the files your task names. If you need to touch another file, stop and report it as blocked.
- Never merge, rebase onto, or push to the base branch. The orchestrator integrates.
- Commit on your branch only when your task says to.
- End your final message with exactly one of these envelopes:

```text
SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE
task: <task-id>
summary: <one-line outcome>
files: <comma-separated paths or none>
checks: <commands and outcomes, both runs>
handoff: <next-step context or none>
```

```text
SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED
task: <task-id>
reason: <specific blocker>
needs: <decision, access, or dependency required>
```
# PROBLEM.md

The problem Betterlook solves. Every change in this repository serves it. When a doc, a habit or an Onlook feature conflicts with this file, this file wins.

## Statement

**Betterlook** is a visual editor where designers describe a UI change in plain language and an AI agent edits the real code of their React app. Onlook already makes the edit. It does not know whether the edit was good. Today an edit can break the build, touch code outside the request, regress the layout, behave differently on a second run, or follow an instruction hidden in a file or web page, and the designer is the one who finds out.

**We are handling evals.** The job is to make Betterlook's agent measurably controlled and confident, without the designer seeing any of the machinery:

- Learn how the agent actually fails by reading real traces, before choosing any metric.
- Check every edit against the real outcome (build, diff scope, rendered UI) with deterministic checks first, and narrow, human-calibrated judges only where code can't decide.
- Block regressions before merge, and measure reliability across repeated runs (`pass^k`), not one lucky run.
- Trace every session with secrets redacted, so real failures become new test cases.
- Prove that prompt and harness changes improve the agent on a frozen suite, across the models users choose.

## Constraints

- No model training of any kind.
- Users bring their own model keys.
- The team writes every rubric, judge, label and safety fixture by hand.
- The frontend is a new minimal Astryx shell.
- Cut anything not driven by an observed failure.

## The failures we know of

These are the failures the statement names. A new one joins this list only from a real trace.

| Failure | What the designer sees today |
|---|---|
| Build breaks | The app stops rendering after the edit. |
| Out-of-scope diff | Files or code the request never mentioned changed. |
| Layout regression | Something other than the requested element moved or broke. |
| Nondeterminism | The same request gives a different result on a second run. |
| Prompt injection | The agent followed an instruction found in a file or web page, not the designer's. |

## Done means

- A designer's edit is checked against the build, the diff and the rendered UI before they are told it worked.
- A prompt or harness change merges only if it does no worse on the frozen suite, measured as `pass^k`, on every model users can pick.
- Every session leaves a redacted trace, and a failure found in one can become a test case.
- None of this adds a screen, a control or a wait the designer has to manage.

## Decisions

- Betterlook is a web app, built from scratch, frontend and agent backend alike. No Onlook code is reused; Onlook is only the product we measure against.
- English only. No translations, no changesets.

# Errors and recovery

Copy Page

Handle declined consent, admission failures, Responses errors, and revoked sessions.

## ChatGPT plan use isn’t enabled

This branch applies when consent is declined or the OAuth result lacks permission to use the user’s ChatGPT plan. Do not proceed to inference on this path.

After a successful OAuth exchange, check the returned scopes for `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`. If the result contains a valid ID token without that permission, retain the sign-in but mark ChatGPT plan usage as disabled. A coding harness still needs a way to pay for inference, so offer a clear choice: enable ChatGPT plan usage or configure another supported billing path, such as the user’s own API key.

When the user explicitly chooses to enable ChatGPT plan usage from your tool’s settings, including after an earlier decline, repeat OAuth with the saved client ID and the complete requested scope set, explicitly including `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`. Request consent with `force_reconsent=true` only after OpenAI confirms deployment for your integration; the existing OAuth `prompt=consent` mechanism remains supported before that rollout. Your app should not force consent on every ordinary sign-in. Recheck the granted scopes afterward. These are OAuth authorization parameters, not the unsupported Responses request-body `prompt` field.

## Errors and connection recovery

ChatGPT plan usage errors stop inference. OpenAI does not silently switch the request to another billing path. Preserve the actual HTTP status, response body shape, error code when present, and request ID.

### Before a stream opens

Do not assume every failure has the standard API `error` object. Direct-route admission can return a body such as `{"detail":"..."}` before a Responses request starts. Treat the message as diagnostic text, not a stable machine-readable code.

Direct-admission status  | Recovery
--- | ---
`401`  | The required signed identity or direct permission was not accepted. Check the selected ChatGPT account and granted scopes.
`403`  | A policy or permission check, such as the permitted serving region, prevented admission. Surface the restriction and verify the integration.
`503`  | Direct routing is unavailable or not enabled. Preserve credentials and use bounded backoff for temporary failures.

### Structured Responses errors

When a Responses-layer error object is returned, use its exact `error.code` and `error.param`. The following codes have specific recovery actions; they are not an exhaustive list of authentication, routing, or transport failures.

Returned code  | HTTP status  | What to do
--- | --- | ---
`subscription_sharing_user_not_eligible`  | 403  | ChatGPT plan usage is unavailable for the selected user, workspace, or policy. Explain the restriction; do not repeat the same request or loop through OAuth.
`subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded`  | 429  | Pause new requests that use the user’s ChatGPT plan and link to ChatGPT settings → Usage. Do not assume the entire plan is empty or infer a reset time from this code alone; an app-specific limit can also apply.
`subscription_sharing_usage_unavailable`  | 503  | Usage availability could not be checked. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Quickstart

Copy Page

Choose a Sign in with ChatGPT integration for your website, plugin, or open-source client.

Sign in with ChatGPT lets users sign in to your app with their ChatGPT account and, when eligible, use their ChatGPT plan for AI requests. It supports sign-in and optional ChatGPT plan usage:

  * For users: Sign in with an existing ChatGPT account. Eligible ChatGPT Plus and Pro users can use their ChatGPT plan for AI requests in participating apps and manage app usage and access in ChatGPT settings.
  * For partner apps: Offer a familiar sign-in option on your website or in your ChatGPT plugin. Apps approved for ChatGPT plan usage can also complete eligible AI requests with usage included in the user’s ChatGPT plan or available credits.
  * For open-source developers: Let users run AI workloads in your tools with their ChatGPT plan, without requiring them to provide an API key. The open-source sign-in flow registers your client and issues OAuth credentials for eligible Responses API requests, without a client secret or partner API key.

Sign in with ChatGPT is currently available to selected commercial partners through a limited trial. ChatGPT plan usage is available to all open-source partners and selected private clients.

## Choose an integration

Start here  | What it is
--- | ---
Sign-in on your website  | ChatGPT users bring their identity into your product to sign up or sign in with an account they already use.
Sign-in for your ChatGPT plugin  | Users sign in to your app through ChatGPT with less OAuth friction.
ChatGPT plan usage in your open-source app  | Eligible ChatGPT Plus and Pro users can use their ChatGPT plan for AI requests in your product.

## Make sign-in recognizable

Label the action Continue with ChatGPT. Place it with your other sign-in options, give it comparable visual prominence, and use approved OpenAI branding.

Returning users should find the same sign-in method on subsequent visits. If someone already has an account, provide a clear way to confirm and link it. When your product requires enterprise single sign-on, guide the person to that existing sign-in experience.

## Understand scopes

With the appropriate identity scopes, your application can receive a stable account identifier and a person’s name, email address, and profile picture. Identity scopes don’t grant access to ChatGPT conversations or OpenAI API resources.

Using a ChatGPT plan requires separate Responses API scopes that the user must authorize. It doesn’t grant access to the user’s API key or conversations. Follow the open-source sign-in guide for its authorization and request contract.

## Follow the sign-in flow

Identity-only clients request `openid profile email` to receive an ID token for sign-in. Clients that use ChatGPT plans also request scopes for Responses API access. If the user grants those scopes, the token response includes an access token for eligible inference requests.

  1. Your application starts an OpenID Connect sign-in with PKCE.
  2. The person authenticates and consents with OpenAI.
  3. OpenAI returns an authorization code to your registered callback.
  4. Your backend exchanges the code and verifies the OpenAI ID token.
  5. Your application identifies or creates a local account and issues its own session.

For a plugin, your application also returns a connector authorization code to ChatGPT. The connector’s permissions and credentials remain separate from the OpenAI identity token.

Your application owns account creation, enterprise sign-in policy, sessions, authorization, and connector access. Sign in with ChatGPT supplies the verified OpenAI identity used by those application flows.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# On your website

Copy Page

Add Sign in with ChatGPT using Authorization Code with PKCE and OpenID Connect.

Sign in with ChatGPT is currently available to selected commercial partners through a limited trial. To join the waitlist, contact your OpenAI representative.

Add Continue with ChatGPT to your website using the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE and OpenID Connect. Your backend exchanges the authorization code, verifies the OpenAI ID token, associates the verified issuer, client ID, and subject (`sub`) with an application account, and creates its own session.

## Before you begin

Request an OAuth client. You need:

  * An OpenAI client ID, typically beginning with `oaiapp_`.
  * An exact registered callback URL for each environment.
  * The OpenAI issuer and corresponding authorization, token, and JWKS endpoints.
  * Your registered token-endpoint authentication method and, for a confidential client, its client secret.
  * A backend that can hold short-lived transaction state and create secure application sessions.

OpenAI publishes its production OpenID Connect discovery document at `https://auth.openai.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Load the `issuer`, `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, and `jwks_uri` values from that document. The production configuration in this example is:
    
    `Issuer: https://auth.openai.com
    Authorization endpoint: https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/authorize
    Token endpoint: https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token
    JWKS URI: https://auth.openai.com/.well-known/jwks.json
    Client ID: oaiapp_example
    Redirect URI: https://example.com/auth/openai/callback`

Replace the illustrative client ID and redirect URI with the values supplied for your application. Require the ID token’s `iss` claim to exactly match the issuer returned by discovery.

OpenAI supports both public and confidential clients. For a confidential client, store `OPENAI_CLIENT_SECRET` in your server-side secret manager. Public clients don’t receive or use a client secret. This guide covers identity scopes; ChatGPT plan usage in open-source apps has a separate authorization and registration flow.

Use a maintained OAuth or OpenID Connect library when possible. The Node.js examples below show the backend operations with Node’s `crypto` module and `jose` for JWT verification. Wire them to your application routes and session store. The sample’s in-memory maps illustrate storage; production storage must expire transactions and support atomic, one-time consumption across instances.

## 3. Handle the callback and exchange the code

If the callback contains `error=access_denied`, validate `state`, stop the attempt, and do not exchange a code. See ChatGPT plan use isn’t enabled for authorizing it later. The new-registration callback supplies the client ID used in the exchange. A successful new registration returns `code`, `state`, and the issued `client_id`. The callback may also include `scope`, as shown below. On reauthorization, the callback may omit `client_id`; retain the exact client ID already associated with the pending request. If the callback supplies a different client ID, reject the result rather than replacing the selected account’s registration. Use the token response’s granted scopes when deciding whether ChatGPT plan usage is enabled:
    
    `YOUR_CALLBACK
      ?code=<AUTHORIZATION_CODE>
      &scope=chatgpt.tokens.use.direct+email+offline_access+openid+profile+resource.invoke
      &state=<ORIGINAL_STATE>
      &client_id=<ISSUED_CLIENT_ID>`

  1. Validate `state` against the pending authorization attempt and handle an OAuth `error` before using the result.
  2. For new registration, retain the issued `client_id`, such as `oaiapp_...`. Do not save `dynamic_agent_client` as the connection’s issued ID. If a new-registration callback does not include an issued ID, treat registration as incomplete.
  3. Exchange the code. POST a form-encoded `authorization_code` grant to `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token` with the issued `client_id`, `code`, `code_verifier`, the same `redirect_uri`, and the same `resource`. No client secret is required.

If code exchange returns `invalid_grant`, discard that code and start a fresh authorization with the issued client ID retained for this attempt. The token endpoint returns the credentials and granted scopes used in the next steps.

## 4. Validate the ID token and ChatGPT plan permission

Validate the ID token. Verify its signature against OpenAI’s published JWKS. Check the issuer, audience against the issued client ID, expiration, and the nonce saved for this attempt. Use its validated `sub` as the account identity. Email and `sub` are not workspace identifiers; retain the issued client ID with the verified identity to keep registrations separate. The signature-validation example in On your website also applies here; this OSS flow remains a public client without a secret.

For a returning account, confirm the new ID token’s verified identity matches the selected account before replacing credentials. Check the token response’s granted scopes for `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct` before proceeding to inference. A valid ID token alone does not authorize ChatGPT plan usage.

### End the renewable session

When signing out, revoke the renewable session using the `revocation_endpoint` from `https://auth.openai.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Send a form-encoded `POST` with `token=<REFRESH_TOKEN>`, `token_type_hint=refresh_token`, and the issued `client_id`. An empty HTTP `200` is the revocation success response, including for an already-invalid token. Stop using the tokens and clear them locally after revocation.

For a network failure or `5xx`, retry with backoff while the refresh token is still available. If you finish signing out locally without confirming revocation, clear the local tokens and tell the user that remote revocation was not confirmed. The user can disconnect the app in ChatGPT Settings. Revoking this session does not delete the registered client.

## Refreshing tokens

Use standard OAuth refresh near access-token expiry. POST form-encoded `grant_type=refresh_token`, the issued `client_id` saved with this token set (not `dynamic_agent_client`), the saved `refresh_token`, and `resource=https://api.openai.com/v1` to `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token`; omit `scope` to retain the grant.

Store and use the latest replacement, and serialize refreshes for the same session so two processes do not race a rotating token.

See Token lifetimes for expiry and renewal limits, and Refresh errors for recovery.

## Credential security

Keep access, refresh, and retained ID tokens in protected local or self-hosted runtime storage. Keep tokens out of browser storage, source control, logs, analytics, and support transcripts.

Never put access or refresh tokens in URLs. Send an ID token as `id_token_hint` only to the OpenAI authorization endpoint, and redact authorization URLs containing that hint from logs and diagnostics. A host ID is an opaque identifier, not a token or proof of identity.

If credentials are compromised, instruct the user to disconnect the app in ChatGPT Settings.

The following reference describes the 10 top-level fields and two nested fields in the access-token payload. The example uses placeholders for account-specific and token-specific values.

Field  | Type  | Meaning
--- | --- | ---
`sub`  | string  | Opaque subject identifier.
`aud`  | string  | Resource audience; `https://api.openai.com/v1` in this flow.
`client_id`  | string  | Issued OAuth client ID associated with the token.
`scope`  | string  | Space-separated scopes granted to this token.
`https://api.openai.com/auth`  | object  | OpenAI-managed authentication metadata.
`["https://api.openai.com/auth"]["per_user_salt"]`  | string  | Opaque salt value within the authentication metadata object.
`["https://api.openai.com/auth"]["encrypted_auth_metadata"]`  | string  | Opaque encrypted authentication metadata for OpenAI services.
`iss`  | string  | Token issuer; `https://auth.openai.com` in production.
`iat`  | integer  | Issued-at time in Unix seconds.
`exp`  | integer  | Expiration time in Unix seconds.
`jti`  | string  | Token identifier.
`nbf`  | integer  | Not-before time in Unix seconds.

The two nested field paths above refer to keys inside the `https://api.openai.com/auth` object.

L950: # Token reference
L951: 
L952: Copy Page
L953: 
L954: Look up token-response fields, lifetimes, and access-token claims.
L955: ## Token response and refresh tokens
L956: 
L957: With `offline_access` granted, the authorization-code exchange returns a `refresh_token` alongside the `access_token`. The token response includes `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `id_token`, `token_type`, `expires_in`, `scope`, and `earliest_refresh_at`. A successful code exchange returns HTTP `200`. A successful `grant_type=refresh_token` exchange also returns HTTP `200`, with a new access token and a replacement refresh token.
L958: Read and save the `refresh_token` field from the token-endpoint response so your app can renew access. The refresh token is separate from the access-token claims and does not appear in the browser callback.
L959: ## Token lifetimes
L960: 
L961: Access tokens are valid for one hour (`expires_in: 3600`).
L962: 
L963: Refresh tokens are valid for 30 days. Each successful refresh returns a replacement refresh token with a fresh 30-day lifetime. Successive replacements have no fixed limit while each token remains valid.
L964: 
L965: Follow 【567†Refreshing tokens】 to replace credentials safely.
L966: ## Access-token claims
L967: 
L968: The following reference describes the 10 top-level fields and two nested fields in the access-token payload. The example uses placeholders for account-specific and token-specific values.
L969: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L970: --- | --- | ---
L971: `sub`  | string  | Opaque subject identifier.
L972: `aud`  | string  | Resource audience; `https://api.openai.com/v1` in this flow.
L973: `client_id`  | string  | Issued OAuth client ID associated with the token.
L974: `scope`  | string  | Space-separated scopes granted to this token.
L975: `https://api.openai.com/auth`  | object  | OpenAI-managed authentication metadata.
L976: `["https://api.openai.com/auth"]["per_user_salt"]`  | string  | Opaque salt value within the authentication metadata object.
L977: `["https://api.openai.com/auth"]["encrypted_auth_metadata"]`  | string  | Opaque encrypted authentication metadata for OpenAI services.
L978: `iss`  | string  | Token issuer; `https://auth.openai.com` in production.
L979: `iat`  | integer  | Issued-at time in Unix seconds.
L980: `exp`  | integer  | Expiration time in Unix seconds.
L981: `jti`  | string  | Token identifier.
L982: `nbf`  | integer  | Not-before time in Unix seconds.
L983: The two nested field paths above refer to keys inside the `https://api.openai.com/auth` object.
L984: 
L985:     `{
L986:       "sub": "<SUBJECT_IDENTIFIER>",
L987:       "aud": "https://api.openai.com/v1",
L988:       "client_id": "<ISSUED_CLIENT_ID>",
L989:       "scope": "chatgpt.tokens.use.direct email offline_access openid profile resource.invoke",
L990:       "https://api.openai.com/auth": {
L991:         "per_user_salt": "<OPAQUE_SALT>",
L992:         "encrypted_auth_metadata": "<OPAQUE_ENCRYPTED_AUTH_METADATA>"
L993:       },
L994:       "iss": "https://auth.openai.com",
L995:       "iat": 1790032532,
L996:       "exp": 1790036132,
L997:       "jti": "<TOKEN_IDENTIFIER>",
L998:       "nbf": 1790032532
L999:     }`
L1000: Treat the OpenAI authentication metadata as opaque; your app does not need to interpret it to store or use the access token. `refresh_token` is a separate field in the OAuth token response.

L959: When the user explicitly chooses to enable ChatGPT plan usage from your tool’s settings, including after an earlier decline, repeat OAuth with the saved client ID and the complete requested scope set, explicitly including `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct`. Request consent with `force_reconsent=true` only after OpenAI confirms deployment for your integration; the existing OAuth `prompt=consent` mechanism remains supported before that rollout. Your app should not force consent on every ordinary sign-in.
L960: Recheck the granted scopes afterward. These are OAuth authorization parameters, not the unsupported Responses request-body `prompt` field.
L961: ## Errors and connection recovery
L962: 
L963: ChatGPT plan usage errors stop inference. OpenAI does not silently switch the request to another billing path. Preserve the actual HTTP status, response body shape, error code when present, and request ID.
L964: ### Before a stream opens
L965: 
L966: Do not assume every failure has the standard API `error` object. Direct-route admission can return a body such as `{"detail":"..."}` before a Responses request starts. Treat the message as diagnostic text, not a stable machine-readable code.
L967: Direct-admission status  | Recovery
L968: --- | ---
L969: `401`  | The required signed identity or direct permission was not accepted. Check the selected ChatGPT account and granted scopes.
L970: `403`  | A policy or permission check, such as the permitted serving region, prevented admission. Surface the restriction and verify the integration.
L971: `503`  | Direct routing is unavailable or not enabled. Preserve credentials and use bounded backoff for temporary failures.
L972: ### Structured Responses errors
L973: 
L974: When a Responses-layer error object is returned, use its exact `error.code` and `error.param`. The following codes have specific recovery actions; they are not an exhaustive list of authentication, routing, or transport failures.
L975: Returned code  | HTTP status  | What to do
L976: --- | --- | ---
L977: `subscription_sharing_user_not_eligible`  | 403  | ChatGPT plan usage is unavailable for the selected user, workspace, or policy. Explain the restriction; do not repeat the same request or loop through OAuth.
L978: `subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded`  | 429  | Pause new requests that use the user’s ChatGPT plan and link to 【567†ChatGPT settings → Usage†chatgpt.com】. Do not assume the entire plan is empty or infer a reset time from this code alone; an app-specific limit can also apply.
L979: `subscription_sharing_usage_unavailable`  | 503  | Usage availability could not be checked. Preserve credentials and retry later with bounded backoff.
L980: `subscription_sharing_unsupported_capability`  | 400  | Inspect `error.param` and remove the unsupported input, tool, execution feature, model, or service-tier override. Do not retry the same invalid body.
L981: `subscription_sharing_route_not_supported`  | 403  | Check the exact HTTP method and endpoint. The examples in 【263†Models and inference】 use `POST /v1/responses`; support for another client type or route is not permission to use it here.
L982: `subscription_sharing_invalid_user`  | 401  | The subscriber context could not be validated. Preserve the request ID and diagnose the credential failure. Ask the user to sign in again after confirmed revocation or a terminal refresh error.
L983: `chatpass_v2_scope_not_authorized` or `chatpass_v2_invalid_authorization_context`  | 403  | The signed permission context does not authorize the operation. Check the client and grant configuration rather than retrying or changing billing.
L984: `subscription_sharing_user_unavailable`  | 503  | User/workspace information is temporarily unavailable. Preserve credentials and retry with bounded backoff.
L985: ### Disconnection
L986: 
L987: OpenAI does not currently notify your tool when a user disconnects the app in ChatGPT settings. When a request or refresh confirms the disconnection, stop using the invalid token set and ask the user to sign in again. Do not erase credentials solely because of a temporary network or infrastructure failure.
